text: 2 Method RSI runs in rounds that follow the loop in Figure 1 . Section 2.1 sets up notation, and Section 2.2 shows how execution supplies a source of truth. Sections 2.3 – 2.5 describe the three steps of a round: diagnosing the model’s own generations, building verified data, and updating the model. 2.1 Setup Let M t M_{t} denote the UMM after round t t , with M 0 M_{0} the starting model. We use three of its abilities. Image generation G t G_{t} produces an image from a text request. Visual understanding U t U_{t} answers questions about an image. Program writing C t C_{t} , a form of text generation, turns a specification into a program. We call U t U_{t} the reader and C t C_{t} the writer. The model keeps separate expert parameters for understanding and generation. U t U_{t} and C t C_{t} share the understanding parameters, and G t G_{t} uses the generation parameters. An execution environment ℰ \mathcal{E} runs programs and records what they draw. A specification s s fixes the content of one chart. We describe it along predefined capability dimensions, such as chart type, number of categories, number of series, color similarity, value labels, number format, label length, and vocabulary. Most dimensions have ordered levels of difficulty, such as one, two to three, or four to six series. A request q ⁡ ( s ) q(s) states every requirement of s s in natural language, in one of several wordings. Atomic questions derived from s s check the requirements one by one. Each question belongs to one of three groups: structure, text, or binding (Section 3 ). 2.2 Execution as a Source of Truth For a specification s s , the writer produces a program p = C t ​ ( s ) p=C_{t}(s) . Running it gives an image and a record of what was drawn, ( I , z ) = ℰ ⁡ ( p ) . (I,z)=\mathcal{E}(p). (1) Verification compares the record z z with s s . It checks the data, text, colors, axes, layout, and text readability of the chart. Accepted pairs ( q ⁡ ( s ) , I ) (q(s),I) become targets for generation training. Execution thus verifies every target, and the reader only decides what kinds of examples to build. The same records also supply labels for understanding. We render each verified specification as specified and again after changing one property, such as swapping two colors or reordering categories. Each atomic question is labeled with what the rendered image shows rather than with what the request asks for. If the request asks for a red series and the image draws it in blue, the label marks this requirement as not met. The model’s own verified programs, paired with their specifications, train program writing. Together, these examples form the understanding data 𝒟 t U \mathcal{D}_{t}^{U} . 2.3 Diagnosing the Model’s Own Generations Each round begins with a fixed set of diagnostic requests. For each request q ⁡ ( s ) q(s) , the current generator produces an image I ~ = G t ​ ( q ​ ( s ) ) \widetilde{I}=G_{t}(q(s)) . This image has no record of what was drawn, so the reader checks its content by answering the atomic questions of s s , a ^ = U t ​ ( I ~ ) , d = Compare ⁡ ( a ^ , s ) , \widehat{a}=U_{t}(\widetilde{I}),\qquad d=\operatorname{Compare}(\widehat{a},s), (2) where d d marks each requirement as met, violated, or unresolved. The share of requirements met is the generation accuracy. We report it for each capability dimension and each attribute value, such as the size of the values, the number format, the vocabulary, or the wording of the request. Correct renders of the diagnostic requests calibrate the reader. Every requirement is met on these renders, so each rejection there is a reading error. We add this error rate back to the generation accuracy of the same requirement. Held-out edited renders track in every round whether the reader reports what the image shows or what the request asks. Optical character recognition checks the rendered text independently of the model, and its score decides when a new vocabulary opens. 2.4 From Diagnosis to Verified Data Fixed rules turn the diagnosis into a data plan, a sampling distribution π t \pi_{t} over specifications. The plan specifies kinds of examples rather than individual charts. It first sets how many specifications to build for each pair of chart type and capability dimension. A fixed 20% of the budget is spread evenly to keep learned skills practiced. The rest follows the diagnosed error rates, with each pair’s weight capped at three times the mean. Each dimension of each chart type has a current difficulty level. The level moves up when its generation accuracy reaches 80% and down when it falls below 60%. Within a pair, the dimension being trained uses its current level for 70% of specifications, the next harder level for 20%, and an easier level for 10%. Other dimensions stay at or below their current levels. The plan then sets attribute values. An attribute value is weak when its generation accuracy is well below the best value of the same attribute and below a mastery level. A weak value may lack training data, or it may be hard despite frequent training, and the two cases call for different data. The rules therefore check how often the value appears in all earlier training data. A value that almost never appears is introduced, and a rare value receives more examples. A common value that is still weak also receives more examples, and the reader receives more examples of it with errors to find. A value that is correct under one request wording and wrong under another is paired with the weaker wording. A curriculum widens the space of specifications when fixed gates are met. For example, it adds a number format once accuracy on the current formats reaches 80%. Table 4 lists all thresholds. The writer produces two candidate programs for each specification drawn from π t \pi_{t} . We keep the first verified candidate and fill each pair up to its share, 𝒟 t G = Verify ( { ( q ( s ) , I ) ∣ s ∼ π t , ( I , z ) = ℰ ( C t ( s ) ) } ) . \mathcal{D}_{t}^{G}=\operatorname{Verify}\!\left(\left\{\bigl(q(s),I\bigr)\mid s\sim\pi_{t},\ (I,z)=\mathcal{E}(C_{t}(s))\right\}\right). (3) Verification also shows where the writer is weak, through its pass rate on each attribute value. Values with a low pass rate receive extra specifications in the next round, up to 20% of the round. Their correct programs are also sampled up to three times as often for the understanding data. 2.5 Updates and Recursion Both updates start from M t M_{t} . The generation update trains only the generation parameters on 𝒟 t G \mathcal{D}_{t}^{G} , and the understanding update trains only the understanding parameters on 𝒟 t U \mathcal{D}_{t}^{U} . The next model takes the generation parameters from the first update and all other parameters from the second, M t + 1 = Merge ⁡ ( Learn G ⁡ ( M t ; 𝒟 t G ) , Learn U ⁡ ( M t ; 𝒟 t U ) ) . M_{t+1}=\operatorname{Merge}\bigl(\operatorname{Learn}_{G}(M_{t};\mathcal{D}_{t}^{G}),\ \operatorname{Learn}_{U}(M_{t};\mathcal{D}_{t}^{U})\bigr). (4) In the next round, G t + 1 G_{t+1} makes new errors, U t + 1 U_{t+1} reads them, and C t + 1 C_{t+1} writes the new examples. The curriculum gates open new parts of the specification space once the diagnosis shows that the earlier parts are learned, so RSI sets its own training space from its diagnosis. At inference time, the generator draws images directly, and programs are used only to build training data. 3 BasicChartBench Existing chart generation benchmarks are designed to rank strong commercial models ( Zhuo et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026b ) . Early in the training of an open model, most of their requests are too hard, so they separate models poorly. On the chart subsets of StructT2IBench and BizGenEval, for example, our starting model answers only about 11% and 4% of the questions correctly (Section 4.5 ). We therefore build BasicChartBench, a benchmark for this early stage of training (Figure 2 ). (a) Example in BasicChartBench (b) Distribution of L0 and L1 Figure 2: BasicChartBench. (a) A request, its reference render, and one atomic question per group. (b) How L0 and L1 differ in seen category labels, title length, series count, and number format. Levels. Every chart has one panel. Open models render unfamiliar words poorly, and learning to render arbitrary text needs more training than our budget allows, so the two levels separate familiar text from rare text. Level L0 has 336 charts, 48 for each of the seven chart types, and 10,140 questions. It keeps the vocabulary of the first curriculum stage but uses a request wording that never appears in training. Level L1 has 140 charts, 20 for each chart type, and 4,300 questions. Its charts come from 14 topics whose words are rare in the generation training data, and they add number formats and category counts beyond the current curriculum. BasicChartBench is never used for diagnosis or data selection, and no request shares its content with a training specification. Questions. Each request comes with atomic questions, and each question checks one requirement. Structure questions ask about the chart type, the number of categories, the legend, the grid, and the geometry of the marks. Text questions ask whether the title, axis titles, category labels, legend entries, tick labels, and number format appear exactly as requested. Binding questions ask whether values, colors, and order are attached to the right category or series. The diagnostic set and both levels derive their questions and scoring rules from the specification in exactly the same way. Scoring. A model’s score is its generation accuracy, the share of questions whose requirement is met, as judged by the initial reader U 0 U_{0} . U 0 U_{0} belongs to the starting model and is never updated, so it scores every model by the same fixed criteria. Because U 0 U_{0} comes from the same model family, we check its trends with an external judge, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, which shares no weights or training data with our model (Appendix C ). We also report the character similarity between the text read by optical character recognition (OCR) and the requested text, which does not depend on our model. 4 Experiments We ask four questions in turn. Does the loop keep improving image generation (Section 4.2 )? Which of its parts drive the gain (Section 4.3 )? How do the text and visual abilities of the model change along the way (Section 4.4 )? And where does the loop still fall short (Section 4.5 )? 4.1 Experimental Setting We build on BAGEL-7B-MoT ( Deng et al., 2025 ) . The starting model M 0 M_{0} comes from a curriculum that goes from easy to hard. The model first learns to write plotting programs. Generation then learns basic chart types with short text, followed by a larger set of programmatically generated charts. Finally, the understanding parameters learn to answer atomic questions about program-rendered charts (Appendix A.1 ). The tasks cover seven chart types that verification can check: vertical bars, horizontal bars, lines, scatter plots, areas, pies, and rings. A diagnostic set of 336 requests in the vocabulary of the first curriculum stage drives the data plan in every round. It varies the series count, value size, and request wording. Every round uses the same training budget (Appendix A ). Controls. Each control removes one part of RSI. Continued training trains the generator from M 0 M_{0} for the same number of steps on the original data mixture of M 0 M_{0} and tests whether the gain comes only from more training. The self-filtered control replaces programs and verification with the reader. It samples two images per request from M 0 M_{0} and trains on the one that U 0 U_{0} scores higher. The fixed distribution builds the same number of verified charts in each round with the same writer and understanding update as RSI, but it spreads them evenly over pairs of chart type and capability dimension and keeps the first curriculum stage. Single diagnosis builds the plan of every round from the diagnosis of M 0 M_{0} and never diagnoses again. The frozen reader diagnoses every round with U 0 U_{0} instead of the updated reader. The last two share the first round and understanding updates with RSI. 4.2 Does the Loop Keep Improving? Figure 3 shows generation on BasicChartBench, with its two levels pooled. The score rises in every round, from 45.5% at the start to 52.8%, 56.1%, 57.4%, and 59.0% in the four rounds. Continued training stays near the start (46.3% after round 4), and the fixed distribution reaches 54.9%. The gain holds on both levels, which reach 60.2% on L0 and 56.2% on L1 (Table 1 ). The external judge shows the same trend, rising from 37.4% to 57.9% on L0 and from 37.5% to 50.0% on L1 (Appendix C ). Retraining one round’s generator with other seeds moves its score by at most 0.4%. Most of the gain comes from text and binding. After four rounds, text accuracy is 88.2% against 56.0% at the start, binding is 27.3% against 13.6%, and OCR character similarity is 80.6% against 47.8%. Binding improves partly because text improves. After four rounds, binding accuracy is 34.0% on charts whose category labels are all correct and 25.4% on the others, while at the start the two differ by about 1%. Structure changes much less, as Section 4.5 discusses. (a) Score after each round (b) Score after round 4 Figure 3: Generation on BasicChartBench (two levels pooled), scored by the frozen initial reader U 0 U_{0} , which is never updated. (a) Overall generation accuracy after each round for RSI and the two main controls. (b) Overall, text, and binding accuracy and OCR character similarity after round 4. 4.3 Which Parts Drive the Gain? Execution supplies correct examples. For each of the 15,320 requests of our first round, the self-filtered control keeps the better of two images from M 0 M_{0} and trains the generator for the same 400 steps. It stays near the start, 0.5% higher on L0 and 1.2% higher on L1. A first-round generator trained on verified charts for the same requests and steps gains 8.6% on L0 and 4.2% on L1. Finding an error does not supply a correct example to learn from, and program execution does. Diagnosis decides which examples to build. The fixed distribution keeps everything of RSI except the diagnosis. RSI leads it in every round, by 2.8 to 4.1% on L0 and by 1.7 to 5.5% on L1 (Table 1 ). Choosing examples from the errors in the model’s own outputs therefore adds to what verified charts alone provide, and Figure 5 shows one such case in detail. The external judge, which RSI never uses, gives the same ranking as U 0 U_{0} for every comparison in this section (Figure 4 ). Recursion follows the changing model. As the model learns, its errors change, and each understanding update also changes how the reader judges them. Single diagnosis removes the first effect, and the frozen reader removes the second. Both stay close to RSI on L0. On L1, RSI leads single diagnosis by 3.1 and 3.7% in rounds 3 and 4, and it leads the frozen reader by 2.3% in round 3. Diagnosing the changing model thus matters most on the harder level, while updating the reader matters less. Recursion also changes the writer, whose improvement we examine in the next section.
